formulaCard.title: Simple Interest & Maturity Value
notes: R is the annual interest rate (decimal).

explanation: [[kw:Simple interest]] is the cost of borrowing money, paid only on the original principal, usually for loans of one year or less.
Formula: $$I = P \times R \times T$$ where $I$ = interest, $P$ = principal, $R$ = annual interest rate (decimal), $T$ = time in years or fraction of a year.
[[kw:Maturity value]] (MV) = Principal + Interest: $$MV = P + I$$.
For time expressed in months, convert to years: $T = \frac{\text{months}}{12}$.
[[imp:Do not round intermediate answers; round only the final result to the nearest cent.]]

hints: Measured in years or fraction thereof.

explanation: [[kw:Exact interest]] calculates time using a 365‑day year and the exact number of days between two dates.

blocks.title: 2. Exact Interest Method (365 Days)

discoveryHook.scenario: On March 4, Joe Bench borrows $50,000 at 5% interest, due July 6. The exact number of days from March 4 to July 6 is 124 days. Under the [[kw:exact interest]] method, time = 124/365, so interest = $50,000 × 0.05 × (124/365) = $849.32. This method is used by the Federal Reserve and federal government.

blocks.title: 3. Ordinary Interest Method (360 Days)

Formula: $$I = P \times R \times \frac{\text{Exact Days}}{360}$$.

formulaCard.title: Exact Days Calculation

explanation: Two ways to count exact days:
1. Use the [[kw:day‑of‑year table]]: each date has a day number (Jan 1 = 1, Dec 31 = 365). Subtract the earlier day number from the later.
2. Manual count: days left in start month, plus full months in between, plus days in end month.
Always exclude the start date and include the end date.
[[imp:For leap years, add 1 day after February 29; use 366 days for the year.]]
Exact days are used in both exact interest (÷365) and ordinary interest (÷360).

teacherCues: Use the ‘day‑of‑year’ table from the Business Math Handbook.

explanation: Apply the blueprint to dissect simple interest word problems:
1. Understand: identify principal, annual rate, start and end dates, and whether exact or ordinary interest is required.
2. Solve: compute exact days between dates, choose the correct denominator (365 or 360), calculate interest, then maturity value.
3. Conclude: state the interest and maturity value clearly; verify calculations.
This structured approach prevents mix‑ups between exact and ordinary methods.
